A shapeless oval cloud with a nearly flat line is the reasonable guess. Here are the real points. A dinosaur drawn by Alberto Cairo with these same five numbers. In a review of 703 physiology papers, 86% used bar graphs, an average and an error bar. Only 13% showed the points. So how much can five numbers hide? Let's hide a star in them and demand that all five still match the dinosaurs to two decimals. Version one slides every point onto its own spot on a star. We got the star and lost all five numbers. The center moved, the X spread grew, and the Y spread shrank by almost a quarter. So what exactly do five numbers pin down? The two averages mark a single point. In 2017, Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice built a search that holds whatever numbers you choose. They chose these five. Nudge a point at random, bias toward a target shape, and keep the nudge only if the five numbers still hold to two decimals. Repeat it enough times, and the dinosaur becomes a circle. From the dinosaur, they grew twelve shapes like this star. This bullseye, this X, these stripes, and these dots. Every one of them has this same ellipse and a different median. Francis Anscombe made the point in 1973, with 11 points of his own. His correlation is 0.82, so the ellipse touches the right wall high up. All four of his data sets share these five numbers, so they share the ellipse and the line. A trend, a curve, an outlier and one point doing all the work.
